catalog_quote: 16. Every syllable begins with a single consonant, or a consonant and a semi-vowel, and closes with vowel. All syllables, therefore, are open and long. ... When a semi-vowel follows a consonant, there is another semi-vowel understood before the following full vowel. So we have two syllables instead of one, one of which begins with a semi-vowel. Thus chilwa might be written chilu-wa, accent on the antepenult. ... 18. Words are usually polysyllabic, and the accent falls, as a rule, upon the penultimate — onjúli, shower; ambáta, to carry; énda, to go; vímbo, at home. But words ending in a combination of vowels, ai, ae, etc., accent the ultima. This, however, is only an apparent exception; really the accent falls on the stronger vowel a or o, and the other follows closely, forming a semi-diphthong, but not a real diphthong. If the penultimate contains a semi-vowel, the accent goes to the an…
readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the works opened, because none of them makes a statement about word stress: Schadeberg 1986 treats Umbundu purely as a three-tone language with no contrastive vowel length and never uses the word stress; Schuchardt 1883 has no phonology at all; Schadeberg 2001 and 1982 could not be opened. One source already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass but not in the works list, Hambly 1934 (The Ovimbundu of Angola, ch. VIII, dictaphone transcriptions by M. H. Watkins; file, pp. 239-240), is the only text found that addresses stress, and it is equivocal: 'Many words received a definite stress on the last syllable, and in others the penultimate syllable received a light stress. The majority, however, received slight, if any, stress, hence no definite conclusions could be reached on this subject', while p. 240 adds 'The vowel of the penultimate syllable is long when the word stands alone'. That penultimate lengthening is compatible with the catalog's penult rule, but the same page reports final-syllable stress on many words, so the catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable entry should be regarded as weakly sourced until Schadeberg 2001 is read.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated place (Stover 1885 p. 5, page image and scanned), and the two corroborating passages (Nascimento 1894, Manual 1922) are also confirmed in copies we hold. (2) But the classification fixed and weight-blind penult rests entirely on pre-tonological missionary/administrative descriptions (1885, 1894 compiled from 1885, 1922 generic); the one modern description held (Schadeberg 1990, phonology chapter complete on pp. 8-9) treats Umbundu as a two-tone language and says nothing about stress; Nurse 2008 (held) gives 5x1 vowels, tone marked, nothing on stress. sources.quote: 'Apparently there are three tones in this language ... Kalunga, according to tone, can mean "god," "sea," "death," or "greeting." ... Many words received a definite stress on the last syllable, and in others the penultimate syllable received a light stress. The majority, however, received slight, if any, stress, hence no definite conclusions could be reached on this subject. ... THE SYLLABLE. Every syllable ends in a vowel ...
